name: Weh
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Glottolog lists only classification/survey refs (Piron 1997; Troyer, Huey & Mbongue 1995 survey); no phonology found.

new_statements.quote: In summary, we have discovered 6 contrastive tonal melodies on Weh noun roots: High, High-Low falling, Low, Lowered High, High-Lowered High falling, and Low-Lowered High rising. The first three of these are by far the most common. [...] at this stage of our investigation, the citation forms of verbs reveal just a two-way lexical contrast between H and L roots. [...] (p.17:) As mentioned above, the high front vowel /i/ has a centralised allophone [ɪ] in CVC roots and as (unstressed) V2.
new_statements.citation: Davison, Phil. 2009. Weh phonology sketch. Yaoundé: Ministry of Scientific Research and Innovation / SIL Cameroon.
new_statements.locator: sec. 6.2 p.27 (tone summary) and sec. 6.3 p.27 (verbs); incidental stress wording sec. 4.1.1 p.17
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (36 pp., text layer, pdfinfo title 'Weh phonology FINAL VERSION', Nov 2009) and extracted doc pp.17 and 25-28 with extracted text. All three quoted passages are present verbatim at the stated locators: p.27 sec.6.2 'In summary, we have discovered 6 contrastive tonal melodies on Weh noun roots: High, High-Low falling, Low, Lowered High, High-Lowered High falling, and Low-Lowered High rising. The first three of these are by far the most common.'; p.27 sec.6.3 '...at this stage of our investigation, the citation forms of verbs reveal just a two-way lexical contrast between H and L roots.'; p.17 sec.4.1.1 'As mentioned above, the high front vowel /i/ has a centralised allophone [ɪ] in CV…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Weh is described purely as a tone language (six lexical noun-root melodies, H vs L verb roots, downstep); the sketch states no word-stress or accent rule. The only stress-related wording is a parenthetical calling the second vowel of C1V1C2V2 roots 'unstressed' (V2 is restricted to echo vowels, [i] or [ə]), which implies root-initial-syllable prominence but is not formulated as a rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Tone: a handful of nouns have low-tone class prefixes; loanwords noted.)
new_statements.domain_note: All data are citation forms of words in isolation (c.1,400-word Toolbox corpus, verbs elicited with prefix ní-); author explicitly limits the sketch to segmental phonology and citation-form tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Davison states Weh has a single dialect ('Dialect on which this study is based: N/A, only one dialect'); self-name [kɨ́-wí]; data from speakers working in Yaoundé 2008-2009. Glottolog wehh1238 / ISO weh exactly.

sources.note: Tonal description only: ch.6 'Tone' (pp.25-28) gives six contrastive noun-root melodies (H, HL, L, !H, H!H, L!H) and an H/L verb-root contrast; the sole stress wording anywhere is the parenthetical '(unstressed) V2' in sec. 4.1.1 (p.17) describing the second root vowel of CVCV roots; no word-stress rule stated.
